planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost; this is one of the largest-flowered waterlily dahlias commonly offered, so give plants a sturdy stake from the start.

directions: Randi Dawn is a long-established waterlily-form dahlia carrying unusually large, shallow, saucer-shaped blooms in soft lavender-pink with a frosty white edge along each broad petal. The tall, vigorous five-foot plants need staking or corralling to keep the heavy late-season flowers upright, and the sturdy stems make excellent cut flowers once harvested. Disbud side shoots if larger individual blooms are the goal, and lift tubers for winter storage once frost blackens the foliage north of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the soil has warmed; this award-winning informal decorative dinnerplate type needs a tall stake set at planting time to support its massive blooms.

directions: Bodacious produces huge informal decorative blooms over 11 inches across in bright orange-red with yellow undersides and petal edges, an effect often described as flickering tongues of flame when the flower moves. It won the Derrill W. Hart Award as an outstanding American dahlia seedling and remains popular with exhibitors for its combination of enormous size and vivid color contrast. Stake plants early, disbud to concentrate bloom size for show entries, and lift and store tubers after fall frost kills the top growth in colder zones.

common_name: Gladiator Dahlia (Orange and Yellow Dinnerplate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the soil has warmed; Gladiator is among the heavier-blooming dinnerplate types and benefits from a stout stake set at planting.

directions: Gladiator carries informal decorative blooms up to 12 inches across in warm orange with yellow deep in the throat of each petal, produced freely for a dinnerplate type rather than sparingly as many giant cultivars do. The tall five-foot plants need firm staking to keep the heavy flower heads from toppling in wind or rain. Disbudding side buds will push individual blooms toward their largest show size, and tubers should be lifted and stored over winter wherever the ground freezes.

common_name: OMG Dahlia (Bright Orange Giant Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; OMG stays a bit more compact than most giant dahlias but still carries large blooms on strong stems that benefit from support.

directions: OMG is a comparatively recent introduction prized for pairing dinnerplate-scale, roughly 12-inch informal decorative blooms in bright orange with yellow highlights on a shorter, sturdier plant than most giant-flowered dahlias reach. The compact three-and-a-half-foot habit means it needs less staking than taller dinnerplate types while still producing long-lasting cut flowers. Deadhead spent blooms to keep new buds forming, and lift tubers for winter storage once frost has blackened the foliage.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the soil has warmed; this award-winning white decorative carries unusually heavy bud counts for a large-flowered dahlia and should be staked at planting.

directions: Walter Hardisty bears pure snowy-white informal decorative blooms up to 11 inches wide, standing out among large-flowered dahlias both for its clean color and for producing more flowers at once than most giant cultivars manage. Strong stems and tidy foliage have made it a repeat prizewinner on the show bench. Stake plants early, water deeply and consistently through summer to keep bloom size up, and lift tubers for winter storage after the first hard frost.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; this long-cultivated dinnerplate variety carries very heavy blooms and needs a sturdy stake set before the plant fills in.

directions: Croydon Masterpiece is a mid-20th-century dinnerplate cultivar still grown today for its huge, 12-inch informal decorative blooms in a warm bronze-orange that often takes on rosy highlights as flowers age. Its long garden history and reliable performance have kept it in specialty dahlia catalogs for decades despite the flood of newer giant-flowered introductions. Stake plants firmly at planting time, disbud for maximum single-bloom size if desired, and lift and store tubers over winter in zones where the ground freezes.

common_name: Mango Madness Dahlia (Orange, Gold, and Pink Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; Mango Madness stays compact for a large-flowered dahlia and features ruffled foliage that adds garden interest even between bloom flushes.

directions: Mango Madness produces large informal decorative blooms around 11 inches across that blend orange with gold and pink undertones over dark, ruffled foliage, a combination that earned it a top score among giant-flowered seedling trials the year it was introduced. Its compact three-and-a-half-foot habit makes it more garden-friendly than many dinnerplate dahlias while still delivering show-size blooms. Stake lightly for wind protection, deadhead to encourage continued flowering, and lift tubers for winter storage once frost has killed back the foliage.
